events.title: A NATO defense minister warns that the alliance needs to learn how to disperse weapons production before it's at war
events.summary: NATO member Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine makes weapons more dispersed and underground and industry's close relationship with soldiers. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images A NATO defense minister wants his arms makers to work with Ukrainian ones and learn. This includes how they work across multiple sites during wartime to avoid devastating attacks. "Our industry is a peacetime establishment," Latvia's defense minister said. NATO militaries need to learn how to disperse weapons production, as Ukraine does, before entering a war to preserve their ability to keep producing while under attack, a senior defense official advised. Raivis Melnis, the defense minister of Latvia, an alliance and EU member state bordering Russia, told Business Insider that industry in the West might not be ready to operate as it would need to in wartime. Ukrainian arms makers split up manufacturing across multiple sites, operate underground, and even move around to prevent a single successful Russian strike from having a huge impact on their operations. But in Europe, many companies run projects from larger factories, which could become a single point of failure. "Our industry is a peacetime establishment" that has been built under conditions where "there is no threat," Melnis said. NATO companies work in a far more concentrated way, he said, and "the question is whether we are ready to produce the systems in different locations, dispersed, and how we organize that." He said this is why he encourages partnerships between Latvian and Ukrainian defense companies, so they can learn from how the Ukrainian companies operate , including how their systems are "built for war purposes." Ukraine has also demonstrated how a country "can provide that reassurance if, for instance, an industry site is destroyed." Kyiv offers compensation for some business properties damaged or destroyed in Russian attacks and is planning additional support. Ukrainian officials and company leaders have been pushing for Western companies to adopt a more disaggregated approach to prepare for the possibility of a wider conflict. Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider that the Russian threat to Europe is so substantial that companies across NATO should "definitely" start breaking up their production more. Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian arms maker Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that some alliance defense firms have sought Frontline's advice on dispersing manufacturing operations. The company, he said, has adapted to "endure the loss of any site." Any loss is still "painful," but the company survives. Operations are designed so it's "as easy as possible to move," he added. The companies making drones and other gear in Ukraine work across multiple sites, including underground, and are able to move far more easily than their Western counterparts. Diego Fedele/Getty Images Oleg, a company executive at Ukrainian drone maker TechEx, told Business Insider that "every day we are facing another level of threat from Russia trying to hit the factories." The company, he said, has to find "creative ways to switch the locations every couple of months to raise the level of security for our people, because, of course, you want to take care of the people and keep them safe." He said the company warns its international partners that their conventions are "slightly outdated." He requested that only his first name be used for security purposes. The CEO of Ukrainian-Estonian defense tech company Ark Robotics told Business Insider that his company makes different components at different sites, something he said is "necessary" even if it's not ideal. A single site is "the best way to do it," but, he explained, the company has to be "smart about it and not create a big enough target for it to attract too much attention or to disclose where our operations are happening." He said this should be the "default for defense-based manufacturing going forward," even outside Ukraine. Some companies are already taking heed. Estonian company Krattworks, which makes drones used by Ukraine, agreed with these assessments. Karmo Saar, the company's head of sales, told Business Insider that for Ukrainian companies, it "would be a lot more economical, cheaper, and better to run this operation in one big facility, but they cannot do that." "In Europe, we do that," Saar said. "And when the war strikes, I think we're going to be punished." Srđan Kovačević, the CEO of Croatian drone technology company ORQA, which has signed up to begin working in Ukraine , told Business Insider that it is "our deep philosophy that distribution is more resilient" in Ukraine. "Distributed systems are much more resilient to any disruption than concentrated systems, centralized systems," he said, noting that the thinking appears to be shifting across Europe. "This distributed nature actually reinforces resilience, even though there are economic downsides to it," he added. Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine fights on the battlefield and the lessons its arms makers have learned. Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Latvia is one of the NATO countries most worried about a Russian attack or invasion and has been a vocal supporter of increased defense spending within the alliance, helping to arm Ukraine, and taking lessons from Ukraine's fight . These lessons are being fed into a new automated anti-drone defense wall and the acquisition of Ukraine-tested gear. Melnis wants Latvian firms to learn directly from Ukraine's battlefield experience and has announced a series of deals to deepen cooperation between the two countries' defense industries. He told Business Insider that he wants Latvia's companies to learn from Ukraine's "proven, combat-tested" systems and combine that with Latvia's "peacetime establishment, where our scientist engineers can work and can develop and bring those two together." Ukraine's wartime experience and understanding, he said, is something for which "you can't just sit in a normal office and build and simulate and create." Ukrainian companies, he said, work much more closely with front-line units than Western firms do. Ukraine's "military industry has established really close cooperation with the armed forces," he said. "We don't have such experience." "This is something I want to bring as well, that experience in," Melnis said, saying he wants to "take those best practices." Deterring Russia, he said, requires strong capabilities and also continued support for Ukraine. Russia wants "to destroy that support for Ukraine," he said. "Therefore, it is important for us to support, and we will be supporting Ukraine to build the victory." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Decision to allow development of 190 new homes in north Somerset sparks campaign for change in the law Houses can be built on floodplains even if they fail a crucial safety test, according to a high court judgment that will be of “immense interest” to developers across England and Wales. The ruling clears the way for a highly controversial development of 190 new homes on north Somerset’s floodplains, despite the site being in “flood zone 3a”, the highest level of flood risk before land is considered a functional floodplain. Ministers and experts are so disturbed by the decision that it was agreed at a flood resilience conference on Wednesday to campaign for a change in the law that would stop the ruling setting a national precedent. As a result, Tessa Munt, the chair of the flooding and flooded communities all-party parliamentary group (APPG), will now meet Matthew Pennycook, the housing and planning minister, to ask him to change the national planning policy framework (NPPF). “This is a dangerous and nationally significant exploitation of planning loopholes,” Munt said. “Tragically, we’ve lost the battle in north Somerset, but we need to change the framework as a matter of urgency, so this ruling doesn’t result in planners and developers across the country making similar speculative housing applications.” Charles Banner KC, who represented Persimmon Homes at the court case brought by the local council, agreed the decision was of national significance. His chambers, Keating Chambers, said the result was “hugely important”. “This decision will be of immense interest to the planning and development sector,” it added. Persimmon Homes won permission despite failing the “sequential test”, which is designed to be the ultimate barrier for floodplain development UK planning policy, after the inspector found 12 alternative sites at less risk of flooding. They also overcame heavy opposition from politicians, local and regional tiers of authority and locals – many of whom fear houses surrounding the site will be at increased risk of flooding. Munt said the high court judgment “flies in the face of everything insurers, lenders, Flood Re – a joint UK government and insurance industry initiative that makes the flood cover part of household insurance policies affordable – the Environment Agency and Defra are trying to do on a national policy level”. The Environment Agency objected to the development on flood risk grounds. But the high court agreed that even though the sequential test had failed, the inspector was entitled to consider the development’s wider benefits and whether it could be made safe for its lifetime when weighing the application. Annemieke Waite, North Somerset council’s cabinet member for planning and environment, accused Persimmon of exploiting a legal loophole. “We’re not being nimbys, we accept we need to build these homes,” she said. “But we don’t accept the establishment of a highly controversial legal precedent whereby vital local environmental protections can be overridden to build on floodplains across England and Wales.” Local people living around the site are distraught. With just a few hours’ notice, 51 residents converged at the site earlier this week to meet the Guardian’s photographer, many leaving work early to be there – and one coming straight from a hospital bed. “We represent everyone living in areas at risk of flooding in England and Wales,” said Sue Gardiner, whose living room window opens out over the site. “This ruling massively increases the likelihood of developers building up near you, without having to answer for your increased flood risk.” Gazing over the fields, Gardiner broke down. “I’m petrified,” she said. “Persimmon claims we’re not at any significant greater risk of flood, but no one else agrees: we’ve been refused by three major house insurers on the grounds of increased flood risk on the back of these plans. “Without insurance, our home – the home we worked hard throughout our lives to pay for so we could leave it to our children – could become unmortgageable, and then unsellable,” she said. “Thanks to Persimmon, our only asset could become a dangerous flood hazard for us – and a worthless inheritance for our children.” Richard Croucher, whose home also abuts the site, agreed. “The value of our home was supposed to fund our care when we get old,” he said. “Now we’ve got nothing for when we’re old and in need: that’s terrifying.” Persimmon Homes said: “Our proposals to deliver much-needed new homes in Yatton were subject to detailed scrutiny at a public planning inquiry before being approved by an independent planning inspector. “Flood risk was considered in detail through the planning process, including at the public inquiry by the inspector, before planning permission was granted.”

events.title: I moved countries for love in my late 40s. I had to rebuild my career, friendships, and identity.
events.summary: The author moved after being long distance. Courtesy of the author I moved from India to Austria for my partner in my late 40s. I left an established career, close friendships, and a life I'd spent decades building. Starting over taught me that reinvention is possible at any age. I was in a long-distance relationship when I moved from India to join my partner in Austria. I first met him four years earlier while doing what I loved best — introducing travelers to India as an Airbnb experience host. We connected instantly. Two years later, in the middle of the pandemic, we became life partners. After another gap for visa formalities, I joined him in Austria. Unlike most people who make this shift in their 20s, I was doing it in my late 40s. It was a difficult decision because I was at the peak of my career as a content creator at a New York-based agency and had built a life in a city I loved. Many people said it was a mistake. But today, after relocating during a pandemic, making a cultural transition into another country, learning a new language , and reestablishing my career in the most unconventional way, we have built a life we love. Our relationship is stronger My move to Austria during the pandemic was slow. While cross-border moves usually involve bureaucratic hurdles, the pandemic made them even more complex. The author moved in her 40s to be with her partner. Courtesy of the author But we prepared carefully and fulfilled all legal requirements. Facing uncertainty together made us more certain of our plans and drew us closer. It helped us build the resilience we needed for the path ahead. Home is something you build together, not a place where you are born One of the most difficult things I had to do was gather over 40 years' worth of belongings into a bag. Doing that showed me how to downsize my life to what really mattered. When I arrived in Austria, my partner's things were still in boxes in our new house. I added my suitcase to them and we unpacked everything we owned. We built our home by making it a space that reflected both our identities. It's never too late to start again The difficult part about moving later in life is rebuilding your old systems from scratch. Not just the big things like settling into a new home or finding a job, but also the small things like figuring out how public transport works or navigating bureaucracy in a new country . The author says it's never too late to start again. Courtesy of the author I rebuilt my old systems, from setting up a new bank account to getting an Austrian phone number, all with tremendous support from my partner. As an independent woman, I learned to be vulnerable and ask for support when I needed it. Thinking in a new language is life-changing I had already begun learning German before I moved. But for the first time, I was in a classroom where none of the other students knew English. But we did learn to speak to each other. Our adult language classroom helped me meet incredible people from around the world who were also relocating. Learning a new language with them made me a better communicator. Careers are connected to what you do, not where you live The biggest problem with leaving a country later in life is letting go of the professional identity you have established. I stepped down from leading the content practice at a New York agency and left behind my identity as a bestselling author in India. But the digital world helped me stay connected to both those identities. Instead of looking for employers, I looked for clients instead. I used my experience to become a content consultant to companies around the world, followed my passion as a travel writer, and published my first poetry anthology. Having a personal network matters The deep bond between my partner and me did not compensate for the loss of my friends and family back home. Unlike when you leave home earlier, I had built these friendships over the last four decades. My first friends were my partner's friends. But one of the best decisions I made was to join a local book club. Not only did it help me to keep reading, but it also gave me a chance to meet people with similar interests. You have to embrace your roots and wings I also had to find my balance between the two countries I now call home. I was still keenly aware of my home country's history and cultural traditions. But I also came to appreciate many things about being Austrian. As someone who had been an experienced host, I learned about Austrian history, culture, food, and traditions with the same enthusiasm. Embracing my new country helped me genuinely value and come to enjoy my new home. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income
events.summary: Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials. Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron ( CVX ) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%. After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures. Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added. Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion. Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows. Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks. Enterprise Products Partners ( EPD ) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%. Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42 . The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong. While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes. Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves. In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said. Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks. Brookfield Infrastructure Partners ( BIP ) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%. Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47 . The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

events.title: Why the US-Iran war is working in China’s favour
events.summary: It must be unique for New York to host the president of a country at war with the US. But alongside Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian, who is in town for the UN General Assembly , an even more important protagonist in the conflict visited Donald Trump: Chinese leader Xi Jinping . What does Beijing stand to gain from the US-Iran conflict ? It benefits from Washington’s distraction. While a third of the US Navy is occupied in a war with no clear end goal, the US squanders munitions and international respect alike. Meanwhile, China is free to expand its strength, deal with its own problems and pose as the responsible, rule-abiding superpower. The current “warm war” suits it just fine. With a strenuous and expensive US military effort, oil and other commodities are getting out of the Gulf in increasing amounts, although not to pre-conflict levels. That keeps up the domestic political pressure on the White House and means it cannot easily walk away. China has reportedly provided satellite imagery to the Iranians to help them target US bases. It has also supplied shipments with dual-use components that Iran could use to build missiles and drones. As with Russia’s war against Ukraine, China can simultaneously profit, make itself invaluable to a combatant, keep a conflict bubbling along, restrain full-scale escalation and maintain the facade of benevolent neutrality. In this vein, China does not want energy flows from the Gulf to be almost entirely cut, or for Iran to escalate, or return to large-scale, damaging attacks against regional infrastructure, as in March and April. It is a key investor across the Arab Gulf countries, much more than in Iran. It has large and expensive assets and many of its citizens live in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and Iraq. The Bab Al Mandeb strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, under recent threat from Iran’s allies, the Houthis in Yemen, is a key conduit for Chinese goods to Europe. A Chinese naval base in Djibouti keeps watch over this strait. The GCC and Iraq are cumulatively far more important energy suppliers, customers and economic partners for China than Iran. Beijing does not need to choose between them. In 2023, it brokered a deal to restore diplomatic relations between Riyadh and Tehran, following the damaging drone and missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities in 2019. Some hoped it would intervene to prevent a repeat. In this year’s war, China might have quietly restrained Iran from trying to unleash more devastation on Saudi energy infrastructure, which would damage its own interests, but it has not emerged as a mediator. Staying out of the morass probably seems wise in Beijing now, though it does impose a hard limit on China’s diplomatic and security weight. It has to be careful not to appear a fair-weather friend, or worse, a two-faced one, in the Gulf. A return to the near-total blockade seen early in the war would hurt China’s key trading partners in Asia and Europe, notably energy-short Japan, South Korea and the Asean nations. Its export-dependent economy is limping; it does not want a global recession. But Beijing is the best-prepared major nation for such an energy crisis, if it continues at a restrained level. Unlike the US, now a major net exporter, it is the world’s largest importer of both oil and gas. However, its domestic coal resource base and its vast and growing renewable and nuclear sectors insulate its electricity system from gas shocks. It can be relatively flexible in its imports of liquefied natural gas, where Qatari shipments have been severely disrupted, because of its major gas pipelines from Russia and Central Asia. In turn, Moscow’s decision to torpedo its core European gas market has left it reliant on its giant eastern neighbour. Another ill-judged decision to go to war has contributed to Chinese ascendancy. Last year, almost as if Beijing foresaw what was coming, it accumulated huge strategic stocks of oil, which it has been gradually drawing down since the start of the war. Its state-directed energy system has proven a useful tool in meeting national priorities. It continues to electrify its road transport, gradually reducing its need for petroleum. And its juggernaut of a clean-tech sector continues to gain from the war. Six of the top seven electric vehicle makers worldwide are Chinese. It accounts for about 79 per cent of the world’s wind turbine market, 80 per cent of the global solar photovoltaic market, and 80 to 90 per cent of core components for lithium-ion batteries. Independent Chinese refiners did benefit from the opportunity to import cut-price Iranian crude. With the effective US maritime blockade, the last dribs of that are arriving. We still have to see whether China will help its friend weather the embargo, or somehow enable more Iranian oil to evade the stranglehold. After losing an ally in Venezuela in January, it will not want to see another leading oil exporter forced to bow to America. On August 24, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “Economic D-Day” against Iran. But notably, the tougher sanctions have not specifically targeted China, which remains Tehran’s key trading partner and essentially the only remaining customer for its oil. Some previous American measures have hit individual Chinese independent refineries and oil terminals, but none of the major or systemically important ones. China has enacted counter-sanctions, which would target companies complying with US restrictions, presenting them with a tricky choice. This resembles the European Union’s blocking statute, first introduced in 1996 and revived in 2018. But Brussels has never had the guts to wield this weapon seriously; Beijing will. It has leverage over the US, particularly in its ability to cut off rare-earth supplies. China thus has significant influence over the success of American sanctions against both Tehran and Moscow. Of course, things could still go wrong. Chinese petroleum stocks are not infinite, while the US’s mastery of shale oil and gas remains a huge strategic advantage. A breakthrough in nuclear fusion or artificial intelligence might turbocharge the US energy system. The regime in Tehran could collapse under the strains of war and sanctions, and hand the US another invaluable Middle Eastern ally. For all its strengths, China’s state-centric economy has serious long-term weaknesses. It cannot shrug off a severe shortage of oil indefinitely, in combination with its huge debt overhang, a real estate slump, an ageing workforce, and an over-reliance on exports in a suspicious world. Yet, as US secretary of state Madeleine Albright said in 1998, “We are the indispensable nation. We stand tall, and we see further than other countries into the future.” Now she might have been speaking from the Great Hall of the People by Tiananmen Square.

events.title: The British military is feeding a 'load of data' from the war in Ukraine into its next-gen Challenger 3 main battle tank
events.summary: The next-generation Challenger 3 tank is absorbing lessons from the war. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land/Screengrab via YouTube Britain's next-generation main battle tank is being developed and enhanced amid the war in Ukraine. The new tank is a fully modernized version of the decades-old Challenger 2, which Ukraine operates. It will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with NATO. As drones completely reshape how armored vehicles are used on the battlefield in Ukraine, the developers behind the British Army's next-generation tank are taking these lessons into account. Britain's Challenger 3 main battle tank is intended as a major upgrade over its predecessor, which is in service with both the British Army and the Ukrainian military. The new tank will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with other NATO forces . "We're taking a load of data from Ukraine" and feeding it into the Challenger 3 development, a UK defense ministry spokesperson told Business Insider at an exhibition near London last week. The tank has a smart targeting system built primarily for combating enemy armor, but it can be adapted to detect hostile drones, a major threat on the modern battlefield. For protection, the tank is equipped with explosive reactive armor. New features for the Challenger 3 are modular, meaning they can be swapped in and out, the spokesperson said, adding that Britain has options for drone-related equipment that can be installed as needed. British Army officers told Business Insider at the UK defense industry exhibition that the UK is learning lessons from Ukraine, not only for the development of the Challenger 3, but for armored vehicles in general, like how they can remain survivable on a modern battlefield. The officers emphasized that the version of the new Challenger 3 tank that exists today is not a finished product; the core platform will continue to be improved to keep pace with changes in modern warfare. The Challenger 3 is the successor to the decades-old Challenger 2. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land/Screengrab via YouTube In 2021, the UK defense ministry awarded Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land a $1 billion contract to upgrade roughly 150 Challenger 2 tanks , which entered service with the British Army nearly three decades ago and have seen combat in the Middle East and Ukraine. The new upgraded tanks, designated as Challenger 3s, were designed as digital fighting vehicles with state-of-the-art targeting, fire-control, surveillance, and survivability systems. One of the biggest changes is the addition of a 120mm L55A1 smoothbore main gun that fires NATO-standard ammunition , replacing the Challenger 2's rifled gun that used ammunition unique to Britain. Other improvements include a redesigned turret, better thermal imaging, enhanced armor, and upgrades to the tank's engine, suspension, and other key systems. There are seven Challenger 3 prototypes, and an eighth is in production. The tanks have already completed their first crewed live-firing trials and are undergoing additional testing before expected delivery next year, which was pushed back from 2025. The Challenger 3 is at the center of what British Army officers and officials describe as the new "20-40-40" model, a layered approach to armor operations designed to protect high-value assets such as tanks and helicopters by relying more on cheaper drones and robots . The defense ministry spokesperson said this approach was taken directly from Ukraine, where cheap drones worth hundreds of dollars have been able to destroy armored vehicles that cost millions. The 20-40-40 model underscores that while the war in Ukraine has raised questions about the utility of tanks and other armored vehicles on modern battlefields, British military leaders still see them as a core part of their strategy. events.title: My husband has been going on the same family trip every year since he was a baby. Now, we get to bring our daughter.
events.summary: The author's husband goes to the same place every summer for a family reunion. Last year, their daughter joined for the first time. Courtesy of Riana Ang-Canning My husband's family goes to the same place every year for a family reunion. I started going with him in 2015, and last year, our daughter went for the first time. I'm excited to continue the family tradition with the next generation. Every year, my husband's family gathers on the Sunshine Coast of British Columbia, Canada, for a long weekend family reunion . They fish, swim, hike, roast marshmallows around the campfire, and catch up on the back deck. The weekend culminates in the annual horseshoe tournament, where the winners add their names to the trophy and we all celebrate with a potluck roast dinner . My husband, Colin, has been going up to the Sunshine Coast every year since he was a baby. There's a tree on the property that he planted in elementary school that now stands over 40 feet tall. I started attending with him in 2015, first as his girlfriend and then in 2022, as his wife. And now we get to share this annual family tradition with our daughter. Last year, our daughter joined the family trip for the first time In 2025, we got to bring our daughter up to the Sunshine Coast for the first time. Not only was it her first time joining the family trip, but at 5 months old, it was her first trip ever. It was so fun to bring our daughter along and to introduce her to my husband's extended family . We spent most of our trip out on the back deck, where our daughter lay on a blanket, entertaining her relatives. The fresh air even helped her sleep through the night! In between naps and nursing, we squeezed in a family hike and a quick swim. But overall, it was a very laid-back vacation with our baby. The couple enjoys seeing their daughter experience the Sunshine Coast. Courtesy of Riana Ang-Canning This year, with a toddler, it was a completely different trip When we headed back up to the Sunshine Coast in July 2026, we knew it was going to be a totally different trip than the year before. This time, we had an 18-month-old toddler who was on the move, eating full meals, and only napping once per day. It was a lot more work to keep up with our daughter this year. Colin and I were constantly checking that someone was with her and taking inventory of everything she might need (toys, snacks, a life jacket, a water bottle, etc.). But it was also a lot of fun. Last year, she wasn't crawling or walking . But this year, she was running across grass fields, sitting in her own child-size camping chair, and helping herself to snacks from the kitchen. My favorite part of this year's trip was seeing our daughter bond with her cousins. She was enamored by the big kids, and they totally took her under their wing. I loved watching her play piano with them and hold hands as they walked down trails together. We can't wait to continue this family tradition with the next generation When I first joined my husband's annual family trip in 2015, I knew I was so lucky to have this beautiful place to visit every year in the company of the nicest people. The Sunshine Coast became one of my favorite places in the world. And now the trip is that much more meaningful because we get to share it with our daughter. I love that we're passing on this family tradition to the next generation and that we'll be able to mark the years of her life in annual trips to the Sunshine Coast. This year, she was thrilled to meet the goats who live next door, go out on the boat to check crab traps, and blow bubbles with her cousins. I can't wait to see what she experiences on our trip next year! Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Meta data center in Louisiana is creating a housing boom
events.summary: Meta is building its Hyperion data center in Holly Ridge, Louisiana. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Meta is building its largest AI data center to date in northeast Louisiana. More than 7,500 trade workers will be on-site at the data center at peak construction. A local housing gap has spurred a boom in mobile home parks like Antley Pines. For decades, Richland Parish remained a small farming community nestled in Louisiana's northeast corner. Residents living in the parish — a spattering of rural towns and unincorporated communities — had come to know their home for its slower pace of life. Much of the area is filled with winding back roads, sprawling farmland, and a skyline free of towering skyscrapers. The closest major regional city is Monroe, about 30 minutes west, with a population more than twice that of Richland Parish. It's the kind of place where everybody claims to know everybody, or at very least, has heard of them. Now Meta has arrived , and things are changing. In December 2024, the company announced plans to build its largest data center to date in Richland Parish, specifically near the unincorporated community of Holly Ridge, which local outlets report has fewer than 2,000 residents. Meta said the $50 billion, multi-year project would support around 7,500 jobs at the peak of construction and around 1,000 operational jobs, eclipsing the local community by thousands. Angel Crawford of Delhi, a town about 10 minutes west of Holly Ridge, first noticed a surge in construction and operational workers arriving in her community last year. Around that time, she and her husband, Bryan, opened a mobile home park to help address the housing gap. Angel and Bryan Crawford founded Antley Pines. Angel Crawford Bryan and Angel Crawford initially worked in the nursing industry, but pivoted careers in 2024 after becoming empty nesters. "We started with real estate and rentals because they are very much needed in this area," Angel told Business Insider. "It's very rural here, so when there are fluctuating prices in the market, it doesn't really hit us because there are never enough houses for sale or rent." They began buying older homes and fixer-uppers that year. "We had a vision to create a mobile home park, and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center. That's what pushed us to keep going forward, " Angel said. "We understood there wasn't enough housing for residents, and our dream of building more multifamily houses was right in line to do that." In 2024, the couple founded Parish Line Properties, which operates 18 homes in the area, including a mobile home park called Antley Pines. Of the 18 homes, 14 are considered workforce housing. Many residents in the park are contractors working for Meta. Business Insider In many ways, Richland Parish is a microcosm of the debate about data centers across the US. Some Americans are optimistic about data centers, citing new jobs, revitalized economies, and the securing of the country's lead over China in AI development. Others are more critical, expressing concerns about the environment, the strain on utility grids, and how the acceleration of AI could impact the job market. "Around here, people feel one way or the other about the data center. Either people are excited about the opportunities, or they hate them. There's no in between," Angel said. "I see it as an opportunity for us to have more experiences in our area and jobs for our children, so they can stay here instead of moving away." The Crawfords opened Antley Pines in December 2025. Despite some locals' mixed feelings about the data center, the demand for housing is undeniable. "All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. She said many of her tenants are subcontractors, like electricians, working with Meta. The mobile home park is 15 minutes from Meta's construction site. Business Insider Although Antley Pines isn't directly in Holly Ridge, the mobile park is still reaping the economic benefits. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," Angel said. That kind of routine can take a toll on workers, many of whom are not from the area. "One of the big things my tenants tell me is that if they live in Dallas and it's 30 miles to work, it takes about 30 minutes. Well, in rural areas, 30 miles could take 60 minutes because of all the back roads and little towns you have to go through," she said. "The closer they can get to the job site, the better." The influx of workers has boosted market prices. Angel Crawford Antley Pines offers fully furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom homes, which Angel said gives workers the option of staying with family or rooming with colleagues. She said the homes, which come with amenities, cost an average of $3,000 a month with utilities. "I don't have any problem with getting tenants in those homes at that price point," Angel said. "Before Meta arrived, an unfurnished house without utilities in the same area would probably go for around $1,200 to $1,500 a month." In Richland Parish, the median household income was around $53,000 in 2024. "We've assured our local long-term tenants that we won't increase their rent. That's not what we're about. We're not going to put local tenants in a bind. We're going to find different and new properties to help with workforce housing," she said. Amenities like WiFi are in high demand. Angel Crawford Angel said there are a few common requests among the construction and operational workers under Meta. "As soon as they get into their rentals, 'What's the WiFi password?' is their first question," Angel said. "Some don't have their family here, so they want to do FaceTime." The tenants also value an escape from the bustling construction site. "They're with a lot of people all day long. They don't want to come home to a lot of noise," Angel said. "All of them say they love the peace and quiet." Workforce housing is more popular than ever. Angel Crawford The demand for lodging in the area has continued to grow, Angel said. "I get phone calls or text messages almost daily. Most of them are from my current tenants who have met someone who's looking for somewhere to stay," she said. "If you go on any of the websites, like Realtor.com, not all local rental properties are listed on there." That's what led her to create StayNELA, a third-party website connecting tenants with property owners in 2025. "I did a lot of research for several months by driving around the area and looking at all the different signs in people's yards or at four-way stops that you couldn't read properly. events.title: My sister and I started a small business reselling vintage items. Here's what everyone gets wrong about our business.
events.summary: The author (right) and her sister run a small business together. Courtesy of Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein My sister and I ruin a small business together, reselling vintage items we find in thrift stores. It's not as simple as it seems because we have to sift through thrift stores and estate sales. I don't worry about the ethics of upcycling vintage items because I'm providing a service. My heart flutters every time I spot a unique vintage treasure in the tchotchke aisle at the thrift store. But then I realize it has a chip or a crack, so I decide to put it back. The object may have sentimental value, but it's not a match for my vintage shop , where I always try to feature high-quality items that have survived the test of time. When my younger sister, Hillary, and I turned our love for vintage collecting into a small business nearly three years ago, we had no idea how hard it would be or how long it would take to sell a single vintage item . Most people think it's as simple as plucking an item, taking a few photos, crafting a savvy title, and plopping it on a platform. But there's way more that goes into running our tiny online vintage shop. We had to figure out the best places to source great items, how to navigate moody markets, how to do deep-dive historical research, how to clean and restore fragile pieces, how to set up systems, how to determine the value of our vintage objects, and, most importantly, how to learn to tell their stories. We have to dig, sift, and sort To source great items for the shop, Travel Far Now Vintage, my sister and I love a good thrift haul, estate sale dig, antique mall stroll, or flea market frenzy. But in the early days of selling vintage items, we started with the stuff in our own childhood home . Our mother collected all kinds of objects, from porcelain flowers to royal portraits in filigree frames, and we didn't know quite what to do with them all when she died. We were excited to discover a vast online world of collectors seeking niche nostalgia. As the shop grew, we widened and diversified our search. We learned that consistency is key. These days, we source items three to five times a week. This work has led us into all kinds of scenarios: scaling mold-infested shelves, digging deep into dusty boxes, and sorting through basement barrels. Sometimes we walk away with a bundle of goodies. Other days, we leave empty-handed. But we always shop with criteria for what we're looking for and how much we're willing to spend. Pricing is a bit of a puzzle We consider the item's quality, rarity, and what we paid for it. But it's more art than science. Within an ecosystem of secondhand goods at increasingly competitive prices , we determine the price of an item based on the current market. We sometimes research the "sold rate" of similar items, but that's not always accurate as trends change. The author found a vintage Jack Kerouac novel and sold it on Etsy. Courtesy of Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein I try to land on a price that accurately reflects the value of the item itself, as well as all the hidden labor that goes into presenting it. This includes digging in chaotic environments, restoring objects, researching their histories, telling their stories in listings, and promoting them on social media . The price of an item also includes costs like gas, shipping, and packing supplies, as well as platform fees and ads. This usually means there's a markup over the original price — sometimes more or less — depending on the object's rarity as a collector's item . What are the ethics? At a recent estate sale, I picked up a vintage paperback of Jack Kerouac's "The Dharma Bums," a mid-century classic popular among Beat Generation collectors. I bought it for a very reasonable price in great condition. The demand for a rare item like this allows for a higher markup, and I'm OK with that. It makes me happy to know this book will find its way into the hands of someone who will truly appreciate it. Some people may consider this to be taking advantage of someone else's loss or lack of knowledge. When I buy or sell vintage items, I value integrity, fairness, and transparency on both sides. But this work is about finding gems in the junk, reviving objects that might otherwise be overlooked or tossed. I store and care for these items and then connect them with people who value them. The markup reflects that work as much as it reflects the item's scarcity or market value . It's impossible to sell vintage online without hearing complaints that Goodwill and other thrift stores are driving up vintage prices. But all the stuff people don't want anymore has to go somewhere — and that, too, comes at a cost. Like any other business, charity shops, antique malls, and flea markets must calculate the costs of storing, cleaning, and selling these items. My sister and I entered the vintage reselling world as grieving daughters and remain as enthusiastic storytellers — eager to connect people with vintage items that bring them joy. We factor in all the invisible work that goes into this business, but ultimately it's a labor of love. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he? | Tom Baldwin
events.summary: Tony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he? The former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for all T ony Blair can, apparently, sound slightly wistful when he describes how he once had a cloak-and-dagger meeting with Andy Burnham , who wanted to talk to him about standing for the party leadership. Before anyone gets too excited, however, this wasn’t in the past few months, during which Burnham succeeded in landing the job. The story dates back to 2010. That was when he was a callow member of Gordon Brown’s cabinet and understandably wary of his boss discovering not only his ambition to take over if Labour lost the looming general election, but also from whom he wanted advice. Much has changed since then, not least Burnham himself. His journey out of Westminster and back again – which in his telling has become an almost spiritual pilgrimage of personal redemption – enabled him to shed the New Labour baggage that proved so cumbersome during his previous, and unsuccessful, runs for the leadership. In common with Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer – all of whom tried with varying degrees of success to distance themselves from Blair – Labour’s latest leader now also wants to keep Blair at arm’s length, and certainly far away from his party conference in Liverpool this week. Their secret meeting long ago nonetheless underlines how often, since he left Downing Street in 2007, Blair has had a residual and sometimes illicit allure for those aspiring to fill his shoes. Part of that is because – with the exception of Starmer – those who came after him failed to win a single general election, let alone three. But it is also that this leader from the past still has a possibly unmatched ability to raise our sights, away from whatever the media tells us is most urgent, towards the colossal compound crisis now casting its shadow across the world and over Britain’s future. Blair does not, of course, always make it easy to agree with him. There was an awful lot to dislike about his 5,700 word essay earlier this year, which said Britain had no power to stop either the AI revolution or Donald Trump. It led some to question once more the motives of a former PM whose proximity both to big tech firms and successive US presidents has so tainted his reputation. Burnham swiftly responded to the essay by saying Blair just didn’t get “what’s going on” with the impact of “40 years of neoliberalism” on working-class communities. He later promised that the interests of voters in Makerfield, where he was standing in a byelection, would be his test of what made good policy. It was, however, a bit disingenuous for him to claim that Blair agreed “our relentless focus now should be on domestic issues, and fixing our own underlying problems, rather than on re-running divisive arguments about rejoining the European Union”. Indeed, the bulk of the former PM’s essay was about the inability of this country’s politics to navigate an international landscape being churned at terrifying speed by forces far beyond Britain’s control. Conflicts in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have since put further pressure on government borrowing costs and household fuel bills. It is increasingly difficult to see how the inward-looking vision Burnham has painted so far, largely consisting of new powers for mayors and more regulation of privatised utilities, will deliver his promised “good growth in every postcode” any time soon. This week, his determinedly domestic focus relented and he acknowledged the government must also offer “resilience” in the face of global storms, before delivering a speech to the United Nations in New York on Tuesday night. The speech veered wildly from No 10 North in Manchester to Ukraine, Israel, Iran and China, briefly taking in the climate crisis, before setting out the need to create international safety standards on frontier AI and protect democracy from all kinds of Russian threats, including disinformation on social media. It didn’t go nearly far enough for Blair. On Thursday, his policy institute published a paper calling for Britain to set a course for re-entry into a “ reformed European Union ” over the next decade. Rather than re-run old arguments about Brexit, he would prefer to start a new one, saying the need for the UK and the EU to build capability in defence and capacity on AI is more pressing than it ever was in the past. Although Blair can point to polls showing a majority of the public and an even bigger slice of Labour voters would support rejoining, there is plenty of evidence to suggest relations with Europe have gone backwards under Burnham’s government.

events.title: Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality | Heather Stewart
events.summary: Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality Surging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bind As Labour heads to Liverpool this week, Andy Burnham has promised to deliver “stability” in the public finances; but the economic backdrop is anything but stable. The longer the US-Israeli war on Iran persists, the more likely it is that UK consumers will have to swallow higher mortgage rates and energy bills – just as the government is wrestling with its own surging borrowing costs. We are only a few weeks into the three-month period tracking energy price moves that the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem , will use as a basis to set the energy price cap in January – but it’s been a pretty bleak period so far, with the cost of a barrel of crude above $100 for much of that time. Based on the pricing in energy futures markets, the Bank of England reckons Ofgem could increase the energy price cap, which sets the maximum energy rates paid by homes on standard tariffs, by an eye-watering 24% in January. At the same time, the Bank’s policymakers – from the governor, Andrew Bailey, down – have repeatedly signalled that while they are reassured high energy prices have not yet fed through into wider inflation, they can’t hold off from raising rates for much longer. “We’ve made it quite clear … that it’s going to be harder to maintain that stance, the longer we have high energy prices,” Andrew Bailey said on Friday. Or as his deputy, Sarah Breeden, who like Bailey did not vote to raise rates in September, put it: “The more sparks we’re throwing in the tinderbox, the more likely we might ​have to turn the hose on it.” Donald Trump made clear over the weekend that he has no intention of staunching the flames himself, by bringing the conflict to a close. “I’m rejecting their deal,” he told reporters, after Iran made a fresh proposal. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly … we’re winning tremendously.” With UK inflation already above 3% and likely to rise further, markets are expecting the Bank to raise rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months. Such a situation almost certainly won’t happen – the economy would probably be clobbered into submission long before they got there, and inflation with it. But Bailey and his colleagues are widely expected to make a start in November, the week after John Healey’s first budget. Policymakers will also have to reckon with the impact on prices of what is expected to be the most powerful El Niño weather system in 1,000 years , which as well as being devastating to human life, is likely to drive up the cost of important foodstuffs. Burnham has made offering the public a “breathing space” from higher costs a hallmark of his early weeks in power, with sensible but modest policies, such as the £2 bus fare cap. A new iteration of the Tories’ help-to-buy scheme for first-time homebuyers will follow at the budget, he announced this weekend . But while these offerings show a government keen to help, they risk being overshadowed by the wider picture. With the threat of a surge in energy bills looming, the government is keen to avoid announcing a large new support package, conscious of the cumulative cost of Labour’s interventions over the last year. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” Burnham said this weekend. These include the £2.3bn Rachel Reeves spent on lowering energy bills – including by shifting some green levies on to general taxation – and his own VAT cut on domestic electricity, which the Treasury has yet to explain how it will fund. Yet if, as Trump has hinted, the conflict continues until after the midterm elections in early November, global oil and gas prices could remain high for many more weeks – locking in a sharp rise in bills for UK consumers in the new year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Economists are urging Healey to be bold on energy in the budget, rather than wait and hope. Experts at the research and innovation foundation Nesta are calling for a gas price stabiliser , for example, that would cushion the blow of higher prices now, at the Treasury’s expense – but bring in additional revenue as market prices dropped in future. Any policy that cuts utility bills has the added bonus of bearing down on inflation, helping ease the pressure on the Bank to act. Adding to Labour’s woes, though, the government’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as the global bond selloff has gathered pace. It has been yet another harsh reminder of how exposed the government’s fiscal position is to the vagaries of global markets, with a knock-on effect for the budget forecasts.

events.title: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI
events.summary: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’ The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “ System Error : Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”. When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.” The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world with artificial intelligence . A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their project in the hot seat , forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do. Everyday Americans are up in arms against the AI datacenters sprouting across their communities. Villages, counties, cities and states are imposing moratoria and bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development. Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits, according to a survey by the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society. Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastly more concerned than excited . Interestingly, Americans are generally more mistrustful of the technology than people in other countries. This surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction has, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net. The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch of weird, sci-fi addled plutocrats to pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.” People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhury points out , the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whatever harm their products may cause , depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law. The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters. Donald Trump remains steadfastly on the side of the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which could keep locals in the dark until construction starts. The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said.

events.title: The most pressing midterm issues for rural voters
events.summary: Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey ; Chart: Herb Scribner Cost of living and health care costs top the list of issues rural voters want 2026 midterm candidates to address, according to a new AP/KFF poll . The big picture: Ahead of the midterms, rural voters rank pocketbook concerns above immigration, the conflict with Iran and several major domestic policy debates. By the numbers: 69% of rural voters said it is 'extremely important' for candidates to talk about the cost of living, followed by health care costs (56%) and fraud in government programs (54%). Context: The AP/KFF poll asked 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas how important it was for 2026 candidates to talk about each of eight issues. Cost of living concerns Zoom in: Affordability concerns extend across a wide range of everyday expenses. 57% of rural voters cited an economic concern — including rising costs, jobs, wages and housing affordability — when asked about the biggest issue facing their local community. 67% said they were at least somewhat worried about affording gas or transportation, while 66% said the same about health care and 60% about food and groceries. Three-quarters rated the cost of living in their area as either "fair" or "poor," up 25 percentage points from 2017. Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey ; Chart: Herb Scribner Reality check: Rural voters' unhappiness with costs doesn't necessarily translate into support for Democrats. According to the poll, 40% trust Republicans more to handle the cost of living, compared with 25% who trust Democrats and 27% who trust neither party. Rural voters in the survey leaned Republican: 54% identified as GOP voters or Republican-leaning independents, while 32% identified as Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents. What we're watching: Whether economic frustration affects voter enthusiasm among rural Republicans. 27% of rural Republican voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, per the poll. Among them, 59% say they're absolutely certain to vote in the midterms. Still, 98% of rural Republicans say they're more likely to vote for a Republican than a Democrat. The fine print: The KFF/AP poll surveyed 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas nationwide from Aug. 12-24, 2026, online and by phone. The margin of sampling error is ±3 percentage points.

events.title: Namibia's president eyes local mineral processing
events.summary: The News Namibia’s president has a message for foreign investors eyeing the country’s critical minerals: build processing plants at home, or look elsewhere. “When you are coming to Namibia, you don’t want to be a briefcase business,” Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah told Semafor at an Invest Africa event on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week. “You have to put up a processing plant in our country.” Namibia is a mining-based economy, she said, whose minerals have for too long been exported raw and shipped back as finished goods. The country is a major uranium producer with deposits of lithium, rare earths, copper and graphite. In exchange for processing at home, she offered investors a long-term partnership and a stable place to do business, pointing to 36 years of peace since independence. She also wants foreign firms to team up with local entrepreneurs, “so that you become part and parcel of us.” Her pitch reflects a hardening line across the continent. With demand for critical minerals surging and Washington and Beijing competing for supply, African governments are betting they have the leverage to demand more than royalties. About a dozen countries, including Guinea, Malawi and Zimbabwe, have restricted exports of unprocessed minerals to force local refining, borrowing from Indonesia’s nickel playbook. The goal is to capture more of the value chain, and the jobs that come with it, rather than remain suppliers of raw inputs for other countries’ industries. Know More Nandi-Ndaitwah is also going further than many peers on ownership. Asked whether local partnership would be mandatory for foreign investors, she told Semafor: “In fact, we are putting it in the law.” That promise has a long history. Namibia’s empowerment framework won cabinet approval in 2015 and was meant to become law by 2018. It stalled over a clause forcing businesses owned by previously advantaged Namibians to cede 25% to previously disadvantaged citizens, which was dropped in 2018. Business groups also warned it would scare off foreign investment. As recently as last October, officials described the bill as at an “advanced stage.” Mining is moving faster. Namibia has required 15% local ownership for new mining licenses since 2021. Officials floated a 51% threshold last year, drawing pushback from the Chamber of Mines, which warned against importing other countries’ models. Nandi-Ndaitwah dismissed comparisons with South Africa’s empowerment rules, saying it depends on the approach. She cited tourism conservancies she oversaw as environment minister. There, investors started with 60% to 70% stakes that stepped down to roughly 51-49 with local communities. Step Back Behind the hard line is a jobs emergency. “Over 40% of our people are unemployed. And we are sitting on a time bomb,” Nandi-Ndaitwah told Semafor. “Even when you have your mine there, it’s not safe.” Nandi-Ndaitwah won the presidency in 2024 on a pledge to spend 85 billion Namibian dollars (about $5 billion) creating 500,000 jobs by 2029, a steep target for a country of 3 million people with a GDP of about $14 billion. She framed the stakes in continental terms: without opportunity at home, young Africans will keep leaving. “If they have to leave, it is by choice,” she said. “But as it stands now, they are pushed out by the conditions in the continent.” Offshore oil discoveries could bankroll her jobs promise, or deepen the sense that Namibia’s wealth flows elsewhere.

events.title: ‘China has arrived’: From $1,000 Gucci sneakers to German cars, China is coming for the industries that made Europe rich
events.summary: Gucci built its luxury reputation on Italian craftsmanship, but its newest $1,000 sneakers break with its 105-year-old tradition with a new label: Made in China. But instead of citing the cheap labor long associated with Chinese factories, the fashion house said it picked a Chinese manufacturer known for its “technological know-how” and ability to meet the brand’s quality standards. Gucci told Reuters it will keep making its other products in Italy. But unlike the connotation a “Made in China” sticker carried from days of yore, the move to China is the latest signal of Chinese manufacturing moving into Europe’s most storied industries, like high-end consumer goods and cars. “I think symbolically, China has arrived,” Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, told Fortune . “It’s no longer a place where only cheap stuff gets manufactured and poor quality this and that.” The shift is part of what some economists, like Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok, have dubbed the second China Shock . Cheap clothes, furniture, and electronics made in China poured into Western markets in the first wave in the early 2000s. Now, China is exporting electric vehicles and industrial machinery that compete with Europe’s established manufacturers, while its factories have gained the technical expertise to produce high-end goods for luxury brands like Gucci, whose sales have halved in the last three years and whose parent company Kering cut prices to deal with slow demand.  Howard Yu, a professor of management at Switzerland’s International Institute for Management Development, told Fortune China is following the path of South Korea, Taiwan, and Japan in moving from t-shirts and dupes of name brand items to home appliances and higher-end cars and products “at an unprecedented scale.”  Yu said much of China’s know-how came from Europe. Volkswagen , for example, built cars in China since the 1980s, and “essentially has trained up a generation of suppliers to meet Western standards.” “The moment Chinese suppliers have enough capabilities, then you want to branch out to develop your own brands for better margins,” Yu said. That has left European companies in an awkward position as Chinese manufacturers move away from being suppliers to being competitors. But it still remains cheaper to make things in China than in Europe and East Asia. Chinese manufacturing workers earned $629 per month on average last year compared to $1,341 in Taiwan and $2,075 in South Korea, according to a survey by Japan’s trade agency .  Germany’s industrial giants are losing ground  No European country has felt this shift more than Germany, the continent’s biggest economy and the fourth largest in the world. Since 2019, the mix of goods China exports to other countries has started to resemble Germany’s: mostly factory machinery and cars. This overlap grew more for Germany than any other EU country, according to an analysis published by European Central Bank economists earlier this week. At the same time, China is also buying less from Germany. Last year, German exports to China fell 9.7% and imports from China rose 8.8%, according to Germany’s statistics office , with Germany’s trade deficit with China growing by a third. German car exports to China alone fell by a third last year.  “China has already eaten much of [the] German industry’s lunch and is preparing to start on dinner,” economists Brad Setser and Sander Tordoir wrote in May .   Volkswagen is a case study in how China’s manufacturing capacity has challenged Germany. China once supplied half or more of Volkswagen’s profits , but now the carmaker’s deliveries in China fell 36.6% in the second quarter. Peers Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Porsche posted similar losses. Volkswagen also announced it would cut its model lineup by up to half and cut 100,000 jobs —the biggest restructuring in the company’s 90-year history.  Chinese-owned carmakers are also gaining in Europe, where they outsold Japanese brands for the first time in May, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association . The EU has tried to protect its automakers with 10% standard car tariffs and then slapped on additional tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese-made electric vehicle batteries. Yu said the shift to electric cars also erased Germany’s biggest advantage: the prestige it earned on the internal combustion engine.  “Now electric vehicles have changed the performance dimension towards battery and software, where China is extremely strong,” Yu said.  An edge only at the top Yu lives in Switzerland, so when he thinks about what will come next for Europe’s carmakers, he thinks about watches.  In the 1970s, cheap and accurate quartz watches from Japan nearly wiped out the Swiss watch industry. Yu said the brands that survived, such as Omega, retreated to the top of the market and sold mechanical watches as luxury objects. But the industry had to shrink to make it. The number of Swiss watch employees fell from about 90,000 in its 1960s peak to 30,000 employees working in watch businesses by the mid-1980s. He said the same split could be what’s ahead for Europe as China competes in the areas that were once its home turf. Europe’s moat “is now only sitting at the very top end, whereas the middle market has been all but chipped away,” he said. That leaves mass-market carmakers like Volkswagen with no easy way out.  “If you are in the mass market, such as Volkswagen, selling 9 million cars a year, you cannot retreat to the top end alone,” he said. “The whole enterprise cannot survive on such a small volume, like Ferrari.” Instead, European companies are turning to the Chinese manufacturers that once learned from them. Gucci’s Drip sneakers fit that pattern by pairing an Italian brand with Chinese know-how. Volkswagen has started, too. In 2023, it paid $706 million for a nearly 5% stake in Chinese electric carmaker Xpeng and agreed to develop cars with it for China. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: China and US agree to tariff cuts on $30 billion in goods and AI dialogue
events.summary: The US and China have ​agreed to reduce tariffs on $30 billion of goods and launch a dialogue on artificial intelligence, the countries said ⁠following President Xi Jinping's visit to the US. The tariff reductions will apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood and cosmetics, as well as US imports including small appliances, toys, decorations, a White House statement said. “The ⁠two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods ​in each ⁠direction,” the White House said. The ‌three-day summit between Mr Xi and US President Donald Trump , which ended on Friday, was largely an exercise in mutual diplomacy but did feature some breakthroughs. The two sides agreed to set up a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said. The agreement follows a move by the world's two largest economies to extend a trade truce that had been due to expire on November 10 by two months, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. “This historic visit enriched the constructive and stable China-US relationship, upheld the overall stability of bilateral ties, opened a new chapter in China-US relations, and will have a far-reaching impact on world peace and development,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said. 'Super intelligence' On AI, the ​two sides agreed to hold dialogue on the technology's risks and ‌benefits, with the next round of discussions ⁠set for November, and to set up ​a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said. The ​White House ‌said the leaders had agreed to use the term “super intelligence” in place of “artificial intelligence”. The ⁠Chinese Ministry said Beijing valued Washington's use of the new term. As AI technology continues ⁠to advance, the two sides should step up exchanges and work towards consensus in line with new developments, the statement said. The US and China also agreed to support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation leaders' meeting and the Group of 20 summit, with both leaders planning to attend the gatherings ​hosted by the other. On foreign policy, the leaders agreed that Iran should fulfil its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on international waterways.
