events.title: It's a 5% world. We're just living in it
events.summary: The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher , with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook. The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%. Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption. It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades. Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over. Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government. While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last. Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance. Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation. Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative. The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages. State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans. Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000. Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up. People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust. The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier. The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained. By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills. But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that. In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline. Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time. So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump). The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital. And that adjustment is in its early days.

events.title: Apple buried Copland 30 years ago. Now the failed OS boots in a browser
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The final developer build offers a glimpse of the future Cupertino abandoned for NeXT Asahi fork embraces LLMs and lands Linux on the M4 Mac mini 2 days ago iPhone 18 Pro benchmark boosted by giving it a cold drink 3 days ago Skip the upgrade? iPhone 18 Pro aperture about as unrepairable as it gets, iFixit finds 6 days ago The vulnpocalypse rains iBugs down on Apple with record-setting number of patches 12 days ago Apple iPhone Duo makes developers think in folds 12 days ago Thirty years after Apple abandoned Copland, its doomed attempt to create a modern Mac operating system, a new emulator lets you try the final developer build in your browser. Copland was intended to replace Apple's System 7 with a PowerPC-native operating system built around a microkernel, protected memory, and preemptive multitasking for system services. Three unfinished developer builds – D7E1, D9, and D11E4 – are publicly known. Relatively few people outside Apple's developer community in the mid-1990s ever had the opportunity to use them. Now you can boot Apple Copland D11E4 in your browser and explore the unstable prerelease OS without installing anything. Developer Michael Steil , also known as Mist , made it possible with an experimental fork of the DingusPPC Power Mac emulator . Steil says the 11 patches that enable DingusPPC to boot Copland were written with AI assistance. The upstream project does not accept AI-assisted patches, so the fixes would have to be rewritten before they could be incorporated. Don't expect miracles. The emulator runs D11E4, the final build Apple distributed to developers, dating from June 1996. It remains very much unfinished: if the emulated system hits an assertion, it drops into a debugger and asks the user to continue manually. Apple CEO Gil Amelio had demonstrated Copland at the company's 1995 Worldwide Developers Conference , but the project never approached the stability required for release. Much of Copland existed as plans and documentation rather than finished code. In 2009, Steil assembled an extensive archive of that material in Apple Copland Reference Documentation . There was also a planned successor to Copland, codenamed Gershwin , but it remained nothing more than a plan. The modern Gershwin desktop we covered a year ago is a nod to that nonexistent OS. Anyone familiar with the classic Mac OS of the late 1990s will recognize parts of Copland, and for good reason. Copland overran so badly that Amelio recruited the late Ellen Hancock from IBM as Apple's chief technology officer and tasked her with getting the project back on track. After reviewing its progress, she instead recommended cancelling it and acquiring an operating system elsewhere. Apple considered several alternatives, including acquiring Be for BeOS and working with Sun on a system based on Solaris. It ultimately bought NeXT, bringing Steve Jobs back to the company along with NeXTSTEP. Hancock was later sidelined under Jobs and resigned in 1997. Apple acquired NeXT at the end of 1996, just months after cancelling Copland. The first developer release of its NeXTSTEP-based successor, Rhapsody , followed in 1997 – continuing the musical codenames, if not the code. Rhapsody evolved into Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999 and the consumer release of Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. Replacing the Mac OS architecture took years. While that work continued, Apple folded some of Copland's more mature components into updates to its existing operating system. Mac OS 8 , released in 1997, gained Copland's Platinum interface and a PowerPC-native, multithreaded Finder. Its Appearance control panel supported themes, although Apple shipped only Platinum. Renaming what had been planned as Mac OS 7.7 also helped Apple end the clone program, whose licensing agreements covered System 7. Mac OS 8.1 followed in 1998 with HFS+, Apple's new format for larger disks. Later that year, Mac OS 8.5 became the first PowerPC-only release.

events.title: I spent $7,500 on a full-body checkup and cosmetic procedures in Turkey
events.summary: The author said he was unhappy with the medical care he was getting at home, so he used his airline miles to book a business class ticket to Turkey for care and cosmetic procedures. Courtesy of Brett Holzhauer. I traveled to Istanbul to invest in my health and appearance after a lackluster checkup at home. I flew business class round-trip using credit card rewards I'd saved for over a year. I'm pleased with the care I received and know I paid a fraction of what I would have in the US. Traveling to Turkey for medical care now has several humorous taglines and associations: men traveling for hair transplants on "Turkish Hairlines ," veneers dubbed "Turkey Teeth," and tourists walking around Istanbul looking as if they got in a back-alley brawl from post-surgery swelling. This isn't a niche market or recent trend. Millions of Americans venture internationally each year for medical or cosmetic procedures , and the market continues to grow. My interest in medical tourism began after I wrote for a travel-focused website about a viral TikTok influencer who praised the quality and affordability of medical care in Turkey. Months later, after an extremely disappointing annual physical at home in South Florida, I was compelled to seek medical care abroad. I originally planned to only get a comprehensive physical and enjoy Istanbul . After further research and some cosmetic care, I decided to indulge in a full-body reset this past April. My care was extensive The obvious overhead of participating in medical tourism is travel costs. Because the flight was roughly 10 hours, I knew I wanted to fly business class. Fortunately, I was able to save up enough credit card rewards to fly Turkish Airlines from Chicago O'Hare to Istanbul for free. The cash price of this flight is normally thousands. It was a great deal, and I used it as an excuse to see friends in Chicago for an evening before my adventure. The Memorial Hospitals Group in Turkey offers several comprehensive health checkup packages, which foreigners are able to book. I chose the most basic plan. I'm a healthy 32-year-old male, and figured I didn't need to invest more. The author was able to communicate with staff during his care through a translator who helped him in person and via WhatsApp. Courtesy of Brett Holzhauer. For $1,100 USD, I received: a full lab panel, cardiology tests, a chest X-ray, a dental radiograph, a thyroid ultrasound, and a whole-abdomen ultrasound. I also had internal medicine, ophthalmology, urology, and dental exams. Estimating an equivalent is difficult, but there are now domestic clinics , like Prenuvo, that run similar programs, though at much higher cost. I also found a cheaper dental clinic outside Memorial Hospital and got my teeth cleaned and had x-rays for only $88 USD. For cosmetic work, I had an upper and lower blepharoplasty, canthoplasty, and four moles removed. The total cost for these procedures was $6,035 USD, a fraction of what I would pay to do this near my home. The price tag included an overnight hospital stay , transportation to and from my Airbnb and the airport, two follow-up appointments, and an English-speaking translator. I did have to pay an additional $55 USD for post-surgery medications. I secured pricing months in advance, working with a hospital representative via WhatsApp. The care I received was fantastic, communication with hospital representatives was crystal clear, and I even built a friendship with my translator. During the full-body scan, she was with me the entire time. The next day, during my blepharoplasty, she was with me when I had to communicate with doctors and nurses. When I stayed overnight, the nurses knew what to do, and I didn't need to communicate with them much. But my translator was always a text away via WhatsApp, which was reassuring to me. Throughout my trip, I also opted for several massages and a haircut, all significantly cheaper than they would have been at home. My normal haircut in Florida is roughly $45, including tip; I paid $20 for a haircut, face shave, and face mask in Istanbul. Overall, I combined a two-week adventure with an investment in my health and appearance for roughly $7,500. The author said that some of his friends and family were anxious about him getting medical care abroad, but months later, he's still happy with his decision. Courtesy of Brett Holzhauer. This is the type of care I want For me, the American healthcare system doesn't offer the results it should. We spend nearly twice as much on healthcare as residents of comparable countries, yet Americans have shorter life expectancies. Despite the shortcomings of the American healthcare system, there is still a lingering fear of leaving the United States for medical care. Nearly 100 Americans died between 2009 and 2022 from cosmetic surgeries in the Dominican Republic. When I shared my plans, I could sense people's anxiety over the potential risks of getting medical care abroad. My mom offered to come with me, but I reassured her, and she ended up staying behind. Though some days were uncomfortable, and I flew home with facial bruising, the experience proved worthwhile for me. Now, months after my trip, I'm still satisfied with my results and how much I paid. For now, I'm staying put, but if I have a big medical expense in the future, I may consider going abroad again. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: AI is prompting these Gen Zers to learn how to type
events.summary: Tom Vaughan-Mountford/Getty Images Gen Z grew up with phones and tablet typing, with many never learning keyboard skills. But in the age of AI-driven efficiency — and prompting — keyboard skills have a new use case. Some Gen Zers are becoming self-taught to avoid dictating AI prompts out loud. When Julia Andrusiak was in college, she noticed one of her professors repeatedly pausing his lecture. Eventually, she realized that she was the disruption: Her slow, two-finger typing was so loud that he couldn't concentrate. "It was the first moment I realized that I may not be the best at this," Andrusiak said. So she began drilling: First, she typed out books. That made her faster, but she was still staring at her keyboard. Then, she advanced to touch typing — typing without looking at the keyboard. She's still working on her speed and accuracy. Now 26, Andrusiak has an AI-focused job that involves helping people use the technology and sometimes necessitates writing strong prompts. She still can't type fast, so when she has a longer prompt, she dictates it — and feels self-conscious about what looks like talking to herself in an open office. In 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported that digital natives were baffling "teachers and parents with their lack of typing skills." Now, for some younger workers and students, typing is making a comeback . While AI might seem to harken a turn away from typing — who needs note-taking when you have an agent? — AI is only as good as the prompt it's given. Rambling voice prompts can be insufficiently clear and precise. The rise of AI has some Gen Zers looking for any efficiency edge they can carve out. "With the ever increasingly fast world, we need to type quicker. But I feel like people are really relying on AI," Andrusiak, who happily uses AI as an aid for writing and research, said. "One of my friends said, 'Well, you don't really have to type the whole page. You can just give it short sentences. It's not really that tiring.' But then I feel like it's outsourcing too much of cognitive power to a technology." Julia Andrusiak and her mechanical keyboard. Courtesy of Julia Andrusiak Typing as meditation and efficiency generator Andrey Gerasimov, a 23-year-old computer science graduate , never took typing classes. But he first needed the skill for his video game chats and decided to beef it up, eventually reaching 170 words per minute. As an AI user, he believes that faster typing makes for more efficient prompting. "You're going to be a lot more comfortable actually giving your full thoughts and ideas if you know that, hey, doing this is only going to take a minute," Gerasimov said. He's not the only one trying to up his speed and technique. In his decade teaching typing to 15 to 30-year-olds, Andreas Francazi, a 36-year-old IT teacher in Vienna, noticed that his students' typing skills have deteriorated — but they're setting out to change that. His newer crop of students didn't grow up around physical computers, and their familiarity with keyboards is much lower than previous typists. He's seen younger students come in typing rapidly with just two fingers, so he's teaching them the basics. Francazi said that students of all ages become entranced by a three-minute typing test, falling into a rapt silence. "The practice can be quite meditative," Francazi said. "You just sit there, you have the text in front of you, and you type character by character, and it kind of calms you a bit." While Francazi's screen-first students have mastered the art of two-finger typing, their future schooling and careers might necessitate the manual keyboarding skills he's teaching. Nick Sjolinder, the founder of BYOK — a purposefully distraction-free, digital typewriter device that connects to keyboards — said that around 10% of the device's orders are coming from educators, including elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, homeschools, and universities. A recent batch order came from a high school creative writing teacher, he said, with the intention of cutting down on AI and distractions for students. Tarun Krishnamurthy, an 18-year-old sophomore at San Diego State University, said his college professors speak quickly and tend to power through their slideshows. Krishnamurthi, who began intentionally practicing typing in middle school for fun, has an edge in keeping up. "I'm fortunate at least I can keep up with some of the professors, but I know some other students might have difficulty with that because they need to look at their keyboard instead of looking at the professor's slideshow," he said. And beyond fast classroom notetaking, Krishnamurthi sees his keyboard skills as a potential professional edge: In an ever-optimized and efficiency-focused world, "typing could be a big bottleneck." Slow typing could worsen workers' outputs, he said; his touch typing might give him an edge in an AI-ified world. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ruby on Rails creator declares 'pencils down' on handwritten code
events.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson runs a software company. He's also a race car driver. Jakob Ebrey/LAT Images David Heinemeier Hansson said his software firm was "done writing code by hand." At 37signals, engineers only hand-write code when an AI agent isn't able to, Hansson said. "This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said. A coding legend is waving goodbye to handwritten code. David Heinemeier Hansson — commonly known as DHH — is the creator of the popular webapp framework Ruby on Rails. He also runs the software company 37signals, where he just instituted a new rule: "We're done writing code by hand." "We are going, and have gone, pencils down," Hansson said during the Rails World keynote. At his software company, 37signals, Hansson said that hand-writing code was an "exceptional state," only to be performed when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. When an AI agent isn't able to produce what the engineers want, they can "get the old pencil out and dot it down for them," Hansson said — but then they "fix the machine." "This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said. Indeed, coding has radically transformed in the last year, thanks to AI tools like OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's Claude Code, and Cursor. Some developers call coding agents exhilarating, and they stay up late into the night to build with them. Others call AI coding a lonely or tiresome process . What do engineers actually think? Business Insider polled over 150 software engineers in January about the rise of vibe coding. Over 45% of respondents said they felt they were "keeping up" with AI tools. 17.5% of respondents said they were opting out of using AI code-editing tools entirely. There's only one "serious question" in this moment of coding, Hansson said at the keynote: how to best reap the rewards of AI. "Every other question is below that in the stack of values," he said. Hansson surveyed the audience: "How many people here are still writing material amounts of code by hand on a weekly basis?" After watching the crowd, Hansson let out an expletive. "That's about five," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 5 BI staffers who put AI agents to work share what worked and what went wrong
events.summary: Rebecca Zisser/BI 5 BI staffers told us how they've been using the hottest new thing in AI: personal AI agents. Their use cases include reserving library books and collecting K-pop merch. One editor used it to remind him to call his mother. Muse and Instinct — AI agents designed to help you run your personal life — are the talk of the town right now. So, obviously, we at Business Insider had to try them out. Five staffers across the newsroom's global offices — from headquarters in New York to divisions in London, San Francisco, and Singapore — have been testing both Meta and Instinct's personal AI agent offerings over the past week. Our editor-in-chief, Jamie Heller, got in on the action, too: My husband and I were puzzling over an opaquely described charge on our credit card. We put the wording into Chat GPT and Muse — asking each what it could be. Chat couldn't figure it out. Muse did. Keep reading for our 101 on what worked, and what didn't . And if you have an experience of your own to share, fill out our survey . In response to our requests for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed us to a dedicated safety post on its website. Instinct did not respond to our request for comment. Will Martin, senior editor, used Instinct to pay a car fee, but it backfired Will Martin I downloaded Instinct two weeks ago and chose a very simple task to start with: Remind me to call my mother (she worries). My whoa moment: Instinct jumped to my aid when I told it I needed a new torque wrench for my bike. After a simple prompt, Instinct came back with four options: a cheap one, a mid-priced option, and two higher-end versions — all with links and a pro/con list. In the two weeks I've been using it, Instinct has created an itinerary for a weekend trip I'm taking next year, booked tickets for my daily commute into London, and secured me a refund on an $80 subscription I forgot to cancel after the free trial. My yikes moment: This past weekend, I took a trip to Oxford, one of Britain's most notoriously complex places to drive. Oxford is famed as a warren of one-way streets, traffic cameras, and tolls. I asked my Instinct agent to pay the city's congestion charge after I drove in. Instinct obliged, cross-checking my car's model against the different emissions tiers for the charging zone, and sending me a confirmation that it had paid for two days at £4 per day. As I touted how easy it all was to my AI-skeptical partner, she pointed out that the cost was £5, not £4. So I checked, and it turned out Instinct got it wrong — it had paid a similar but separate charge for a smaller area of the city. events.title: The startup trap that kept this longevity app founder stuck
events.summary: Brent Franson is the CEO of Death Clock. Courtesy of Death Clock Death Clock CEO Brent Franson said startups can get stuck in a phase he calls "slow failure." He shut down his startup and threw out years' worth of code to build Death Clock, a consumer-health product. When a startup isn't viable , Franson says, founders should fully pivot rather than try to patch it. Brent Franson spent four years building a mental-health app that users liked, but that didn't ultimately work as a business. The product wasn't an obvious flop. It had enough promise, he said, to make further rounds of changes seem worthwhile — the trap of something that seemed "pretty good," though ultimately isn't viable. "Mediocrity is so dangerous," Franson said. In late 2024, seeing a need for a fresh start, he shut down the app, called Most Days, and discarded the codebase that his team had spent years building. The San Francisco-based staff then shifted their attention to building a consumer-health product called Death Clock, which Franson, 44, described as an "AI private doctor." Users enter health information — ranging from cholesterol levels to diet and sleep habits — and the platform uses longevity research to estimate the age at which they might die and suggest changes that could help them live longer. The experience reshaped how the longtime early-stage entrepreneur, who in 2019 sold a prior software company he ran to WeWork, thinks about startups. Here are three lessons Franson has learned: An app people like is not necessarily a viable business Most Days had users, though the company could not acquire them cheaply enough to build a sound business, he said. The scary part of pivoting , Franson said, is not when a business is clearly failing or obviously taking off. It is when a product has users who like it and just enough promise to make another round of changes seem worthwhile. "You can convince yourself to keep iterating on it," he said. Franson, who is CEO of Death Clock, calls that danger "slow failure": a business that lingers because its leaders keep rationalizing why it might soon work. One test, he said, is whether founders are working through concrete problems with conviction or trying to talk themselves into continuing. When you pivot, make a clean break For Franson, the response wasn't to rebrand Most Days or look for another half-measure like a savvy hire. It was to shut it down completely. He said the hardest decision was abandoning a company the team had spent years building and still believed served an important mental-health need. Yet, Franson said, the team concluded that they needed to make a clean break and a full bet on Death Clock. The team carried no code from Most Days over to their new venture, Franson said. The decision also meant embracing a name he initially saw as a potentially terrible mistake. The team had considered calling the product "More Years," Franson said, before deciding to keep the more provocative working name they had been using internally. A good product needs a way to reach customers Franson said the failure of Most Days taught him that product quality alone wouldn't cut it. A consumer company also needed a way to get attention without spending heavily to buy it, he said. When Franson went to Most Days' investors about the shift, he said they faced a choice: Take back a fraction of their investment or support the Death Clock idea. Their reactions to the name were sharply divided, Franson said. "People either loved the name Death Clock, or they hated it, but they didn't forget it," he said. Franson came to see the name as a distribution strategy in a crowded consumer-health market, where companies with ample funding can spend heavily to acquire customers. Death Clock's name comes with risks, he said, including whether the attention-grabbing approach will keep people from taking it seriously as a consumer-health product. The episode reinforced an idea that Franson now cites about building startups : First-time founders focus on product; second-time founders focus on distribution. While the company's name is provocative , Franson said the company remains restrained about the health interventions it recommends. Death Clock doesn't sell peptides , he said, because the company's clinical advisors don't believe the science supports their use. It's a choice that means forgoing potential revenue, Franson said. The lesson he took from Most Days was not that founders should never persist, but that they should recognize when it has become a form of rationalization. "It's hard to tell the difference, a lot of times, between slow success and slow failure," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: This small town librarian offers a 'Bye, Bye AI' class to take AI off your phone. Now everyone wants in.
events.summary: Shea Wert, library director of the North Chatham Free Library, will be holding a "Bye Bye AI" event to help people turn off AI features on their phones. Shea Wert A small upstate New York library is offering a "Bye Bye AI" event. The librarian will help people turn off AI features on their phones or email. She told BI she's also happy to help people set up AI. The event has gone viral, with people around the world wanting to tune in. North Chatham, a hamlet in upstate New York halfway between Hudson and Albany, doesn't have much going on. You have to go to the next hamlet over for a store or restaurant. There's a church, a post office, and a small public library with only about 800 cardholders. The North Chatham Free Library has gotten a lot of attention lately, however, after a flyer for an upcoming "Bye Bye AI" event offering to remove the AI features from your phone or laptop went viral on Facebook, getting over 200 comments and 8,000 likes. The poster was made by the library's sole full-time librarian, Shea Wert. Wert told Business Insider that she had made this event in response to community demand — and was surprised by the reaction from far-flung places. "Do I live anywhere near this library? No. Am I in support of this? Hell yeah!" wrote one commenter. The event flyer went viral on Facebook, getting comments from around the world. https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1J7QUQUcU2/ "I had to look at the library's main page to see where Chatham is. I'm in central CA and wonder if we can have a digital guide that our own Mariposa County Library could use for a similar program?" wrote another. "As someone in Ohio who just happened upon this post; will this be streamed or recorded?" someone else asked. "As somewhere near Chatham, UK, I was a little confused at first Regardless, thanks Shea!" a jolly Brit wrote. The library does weekly tech support drop-in hours, and in April it held an "AI for seniors" class that covered the basics of AI and LLMs. But this latest offering was something new. The idea was based on requests Wert had noticed from the community. "There's just been enough patrons asking about certain things that bothered them, specifically Gmail auto replies and auto completes really frustrate people," Wert told Business Insider during a recent phone call. "I went to a presentation that another librarian was doing about this topic, and they had had success with it. And I was like, 'Okay, well, I've heard enough from my patrons that they're worried about this stuff or frustrated about this stuff that I might as well try to do one.'" The library held an "AI for seniors" class earlier this year that covered the basics. North Chatham Free Library That other librarian, Hannah Cyrus, published a column in a journal of library studies, writing that "libraries have a role to play in facilitating patrons' rejection of technology, just as much as in their adoption of it." Cyrus has offered a series of free classes for patrons, teaching them how to turn off or avoid AI tools on their phones and computers, with great success — and a much larger turnout than other tech classes. TechCrunch reported in July that Cyrus's article in the library journal inspired other librarians to reach out and ask for help running their own versions of the classes. "I've heard from hundreds of librarians from all over the world asking for my presentation slides," she told Business Insider. The North Chatham Free Library serves a tiny hamlet in upstate New York, with only about 800 library card holders. Shea Wert One of the groups that reached out was a consortium of libraries for the Hudson Valley area, which included the North Chatham Free Library. Cyrus gave a webinar to a group of librarians, including Wert, about how she ran the "Avoiding AI" class. In Wert's personal life, she admits to staying a bit of a Luddite, preferring to use a dumbphone . But she's not adamantly anti-AI and has used AI tools for work to draft outlines or write dense policy text. "There have been some patrons that I know are using LLMs, and I'm happy to help them with it. I've helped them write better prompts, although that is far less common," she said. "It's more common that they haven't used it and they don't want to use it." Both Wert and Cyrus said that most of the people who come in for help with AI or tech in general are older adults, who are often frustrated by new AI features on the services they already use. The Bye-Bye AI event will take place next week, and Wert isn't entirely sure what to expect given the viral reaction on Facebook. "I'm a little concerned based on setting it up as a drop-in thing that there'll be people waiting because I can only help so many at one time," she said. "But I don't know. If 20 people come, that would feel like a lot to me." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money
events.summary: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft. According to 404 Media’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit. The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6. As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." events.title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
events.summary: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence ( AI ), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”. “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.” Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.” Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”. “There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures. Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate. “It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.” Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale. His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods. Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place. Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI. Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday. The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote. Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later. An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014. Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity. In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’” Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’ “So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

events.title: Baby bank's urgent appeal as demand for help grows
events.summary: Chantal Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 and the charity marks its first decade in January The founder of a charity which provides essentials like Moses baskets, prams, nappies and clothes to struggling families across Leeds has said it urgently needs more donations to help keep up with demand. Chantal Nogbou said there had been a "massive increase" in the number of people referred by health and social care professionals to Leeds Baby Bank in recent months. Nogbou said staff had helped an "unprecedented" 550 families in Leeds since the start of June, and were expecting numbers to rise as winter loomed. "We get even more people needing help then because they want to put the heating on, but they still need to buy nappies and feed and clothe their child," she said. Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 when she was a single parent of four children, including twins, and she realised how many other families were struggling. More families than ever have been referred to Leeds Baby Bank for help since the start of June, according to the charity The charity will be 10 years old in January and Nogbou said that staff had seen a change in the families who needed their support over time. "When we started, pre-Covid, maybe one in five children in Leeds lived in relative poverty," she explained. "Now, you're looking at one in two children in some parts, and that's just a shocking number that really shouldn't be happening." Nogbou said that about 70% of the children they helped had a parent who was working and she said many were "not managing to manage the bills with energy and fuel prices going up". According to government statistics, 27% of children in the Yorkshire and Humber region lived in relative low income families - the joint highest proportion, alongside the West Midlands, in the country. A relative low income family is one living on less than 60% of the median national household income for that year. Chantal Nogbou said people did not realise how far a small financial donation could go Nogbou said the rise in referrals meant more financial challenges for the charity, especially after moving from a city centre office to a larger and more accessible building in Armley which could now provide more services. "All that has cost money and obviously bills for us have also gone up when it comes to the utilities, so it's definitely a scary thing as a charity," she said. She added that it was the donations of items and money from the community that had kept the charity going. "It's the people that, instead of buying a coffee every day, set up a direct debit and send £5 to Leeds Baby Bank every month," she said. "That £5 can buy something like a brand new mattress for a Moses basket." Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds , catch up with the latest episode of Look North . events.title: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
events.summary: Plans for one of Europe’s largest AI campuses in a Unesco-designated reserve have sparked a fierce local backlash The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness. Today, a very 21st-century threat is rippling through the same country lanes as the AI boom reaches the pubs, churches and parish halls of Great Torrington and its surrounding villages. The countryside that makes up the biosphere has been selected by a British company, Xlinks, to house a 1.5GW AI datacentre, one of the largest in Europe, as well as a vast 1.8GW battery energy storage system, or BESS. About 344 hectares (850 acres) of countryside have been secured for the huge campus, with five vast buildings ranging in height from 50 to 130 feet. Listed buildings on the site, Xlinks says, will be relocated and transformed into a visitor centre. Such is the anger locally that the new campaign against the AI datacentre has drawn in tens of thousands of people, uncovered what campaigners say is evidence of secret deals and adopted tactics being used by activists in the US such as Erin Brockovich . A recent public meeting in Great Torrington was hosted by Elizabeth Humphreys of the US campaign group Not in My Valley . She was one of the forces behind achieving a permanent datacentre ban in Coachella, California, over concerns about air pollution, water and energy use. “We’re fighting the largest companies that have ever existed in the world, and that is scary but we are all fighting this together,” Humphreys said. “This is a global issue; we are all connected. People across the world are standing up and fighting back.” Today within the halls and pubs of Great Torrington and the villages of Huntshaw and Weare Giffard, the AI project is the main talking point. And the question being asked is: why here, in a protected UN biosphere, on productive farmland? The proposal was first announced to the public this summer with a call by Xlinks for a collaborative approach. But adopting the tactics of veteran campaigners like Brockovich, people from the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group took to their keyboards – researching, rallying and requesting more information in a series of freedom of information (FoI) applications. What they uncovered fuelled the rising tensions. Documents released under FoI revealed the company had been in closed discussions with council officials since March 2025. In April, the council issued a letter of “in-principle support” before any environmental statement or public consultation – and more than a year before the proposal was made public. Torridge district council told the Guardian the pre-application process was standard practice and was confidential. A spokesperson said it was not confirmation of any proposal and intended to offer guidance on whether a proposal was acceptable in principle in planning terms. In an email dated 18 December 2025, council officials and the developers discussed creating links with a sixth form college in Exeter and a stakeholder engagement plan. “Who do we all feel it is critical to get onboard and when both locally and further afield?” the email asked. Emily Clark, of the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group, said: “Email exchanges and private meetings spanning the past 18 months reveal some officers treating the project as a foregone conclusion. Community frustration is understandably at boiling point. “How can the largest and most costly infrastructure proposal in the nation be conducted almost exclusively in secret?” FoI requests also uncovered a detailed site plan not released to the public. It revealed the two largest buildings would measure 335 metres by 267 metres and cover approximately nine hectares (22 acres) of ground footprint each – both big enough to house Exeter Cathedral 18 times over, campaigners say. Xlinks said its proposals cover about 344 hectares (850 acres) but only a third would be developed; the majority of land would be open to the public or used for new habitat creation to support wildlife, they said. The campus would also house a 1.8GW battery energy storage system (BESS) involving 1,720 containerised units, dwarfing the largest operational BESS currently in Britain, such as the 100MW Bramley facility in Hampshire.

events.title: Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict | Jonathan Wilson
events.summary: Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict Premier League could be hit hard by aftermath, while Manchester City fans may know they took 30 years to recover from a guilty verdict in 1906 So it turns out none of that was real. Nothing that happened in English football between 2009‑10 and 2017-18 that involved Manchester City actually happened. City beating Manchester United 6-1 at Old Trafford? Fake. Sergio Agüero’s 94th‑minute winner to clinch the title in 2012 ? A figment of the imagination. That season City reached 100 points ? Bobby Ewing dreamed it in the shower. Without those successes, City wouldn’t have been in the position they were for the past eight seasons (and 35 of the charges relate to a failure to cooperate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023). The 14 successive wins that took them to the league title in 2018-19 would not have happened without what went before. Neither would the Treble of 2023 or the record four league titles in a row. So while it may turn out that those successes did indeed happen, they are tainted by what went before. “We’re not really here”? Turns out none of us have been for quite some time. There will be an appeal. This is not yet the final truth, which could still be a long way off. But it may turn out that Jürgen Klopp was a lot more successful than anybody thought, that Brendan Rodgers and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are title‑winning managers. Probably not, because the authorities seem reluctant, even if titles are stripped from a club, to reallocate those titles – and understandably: if one side is streaking clear, priorities for others change. None of this feels right, but it would feel off if a team won a league because a rival had chosen to prioritise a cup or European campaign at the expense of an apparently unwinnable title. Ersatz glory satisfies nobody. If the guilty verdicts are upheld, the consequences will be profound. There will be appeals for mitigation. There are wheels within wheels. Bloomberg reported last month that the government had been warned of potential negative consequences for UK-United Arab Emirates relations should the verdict go against City. Andy Burnham was mayor during a period when the UAE made significant investments in Manchester and spoke to the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed, within a week of becoming prime minister in July. But it is hard to see how a systematic campaign of cheating over a period of nine years could bring anything except severe punishment. Everton’s one breach in 2022, overspending the profitability and sustainability threshold by £19.5m, earned them a six-point deduction and they had to pay Burnley, who were relegated, £26m in damages plus £9m in interest. City’s offences are almost incalculably worse and they failed to cooperate with the investigation. It is not just that they could be forcibly relegated; it is that potential for financial claims against City and not just from those sides who missed out on titles during the ghost years. Other sides were denied European places. Prize money was lost. Even relegated sides may argue that City were a factor in them dropping out of the Premier League. There are knock-on effects to the years after the period in question. Leicester, for instance, narrowly missed out on Champions League qualification in 2020 and 2021. Would they have qualified had City, who finished above them, not been artificially juiced? Had they played in the Champions League then, would they be in the mess they are in now? Then there are the less direct consequences: what might it have meant for a club’s – or a manager’s or a player’s – global reputation and thus their capacity to generate commercial income, had they won the league or remained in the Premier League for a further season? Somehow, somebody will have to calculate which, if any of those claims, are worth pursuing and what they might be worth. The financial cost to City, irrespective of the official sanction, could be crippling. When City were found guilty of illegal payments to players in 1906 and forced to sell off the bulk of their squad, it took them 30 years to recover; when Sunderland were similarly convicted in 1957, they were relegated for the first time the following season and have never retained their previous status. But the biggest cost, perhaps, is the one that is hardest to calculate: emotional energy. The Agüero goal was arguably the most famous moment in Premier League history. What does it mean to say it didn’t happen? Even if City are not stripped of the 2012 title, it is tainted. Marseille’s 1993 Champions League success remains on the record, but is inevitably undermined by being stripped of the Ligue 1 title that season for match-fixing. That emotion, the euphoria of City fans, the despair of United fans, the amazement of everybody else, cannot be dismissed. For many connected to City, it must be the greatest surge of emotion they have experienced.

events.title: The ecstasy of buying our first home was short-lived after we found 150 faults
events.summary: Charles and Georgina Barnes bought a new build home in February 2026 It was the day Georgina and Charles Barnes had waited three years for, as they picked up the keys to their first home. But when the brand new property was inspected days later by a Welsh snagging company, the final quality check by independent inspectors, they found 150 defects. These included incorrectly installed fire barriers, signs of a previous leak and what they called "exceptionally poor" workmanship. Swansea-based New Home Quality Control was set up by John Cooper, who became fed up of being asked to hide things from customers on building sites. It is the responsibility of developers to make sure new-builds meet regulations, according to the National House Building Council , external (NHBC). The couple are far from alone when it comes to issues with new houses. Written evidence submitted by the New Homes Ombudsman Service said the Home Builders Federation national new homes customer satisfaction survey, published in March 2025, showed 93.7% of new-build buyers reporting defects or snags to their developer after moving in , external . Just over a quarter of buyers also found more than 15 problems in their new-build home. Charles and Georgina were excited to move into their new home "We just wouldn't have known," said Georgina. "If there had been a fire, that's one thing that could have happened and been very detrimental." Georgina, 36, and her husband saved for three years to buy a house, before falling in love with the development in south Leicestershire. As moving day approached, social media began serving her a steady stream of new-build horror stories After paying £299,995 for the house, she said getting it snagged was "non-negotiable". "It just felt unbelievable that we'd finally done it," she added. "We actually finally got our own place. This is ours. This is ours to do what we want with. It just felt great." But the report also identified improperly roofing defects, low water pressure and what inspectors described as "exceptionally poor" installation of the gas meter cabinet and gas pipe. More than a dozen of additional cosmetic and finishing defects were also recorded throughout the property As they had a two-year warranty from the developer, it meant they fixed the issues. John Cooper describes how he came to set up a snagging company "I would say for any new-build buyer, 100% no doubt, I recommend a snagger," Georgina said. Vistry, responsible for the housing developer Countryside, which built Charles and Georgina's house, said it supported "appropriately conducted independent inspections as an additional source of reassurance about build quality". It said each home is checked by its teams and independent inspections take place and, two to three weeks after customers move in, the build team meets to discuss and agree any snagging work. Such issues are not new to John Cooper, 50, co-founder of New Home Quality Control. He said, while working as a contracts manager in 2018: "The site manager asked me to hide something from a customer that was moving in the next day." This was the tip of the iceberg after he had seen poor quality workmanship over about six years. "From that moment on, I thought to myself 'I've got to make a change in this industry somehow. This can't continue'," he said. Cooper spoke to his supervisor at the time, Lee Challenger, 42, and the two men quit their jobs and started New Homes Quality Control. "We've never inspected a house and found absolutely nothing wrong with it," he said. John Cooper was asked to hide issues in new build homes so he created a company to fight back The most common defects involve brickwork, carpentry and roofing, he said. "I just think that there's not enough quality bricklayers to build the amount of properties that the developers are building across the UK on a yearly basis." The team also regularly identifies missing or incorrectly installed weep vents - which are installed in exterior walls to let moisture escape. Cooper said some developments had even featured "fake" weep vents, where decorative plastic pieces had been fitted instead of functioning openings. "They thought they could get away with it," he said. Cooper said before new owners get the keys, the NHBC inspects the property and sign it off. "I'm sick of hearing every property being signed off, because if that was the case, then we wouldn't have a company," he said. Many of Cooper's clients get emotional when they see how many issues there are with their new houses. "There were some quite serious issues in their new property and they had spent all their life savings on it." Cooper said his long-term goal was for every new-build home to undergo an independent inspection before its owners moved in. "If someone's spending their life savings on a house, they deserve to get what they paid for," he said.

events.title: London’s investment bankers and lawyers make more than £1bn in takeover frenzy
events.summary: Bumper fees paid in the year’s mergers and acquisitions spark anger over high City pay during cost of living crisis London’s investment bankers and lawyers have made more than £1bn from a frenzy of takeover deals this year, sparking anger over high City pay during the cost of living crisis . The value of mergers and acquisitions of UK stock market listed companies has surged 175% in 2026 to $132.9bn (£100bn), according to the London Stock Exchange , as overseas buyers snap up British companies at record pace. Fees paid to investment bankers, lawyers and accountants working on these deals topped £1.2bn, official filings suggest, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets. The bumper fees were fuelled by a string of corporate takeovers driven by a flood of private equity cash and acquisitive American buyers targeting undervalued British businesses. The spree of acquisitions of listed companies has led to concerns over the future of the London stock market . The takeover frenzy has fed advisory business at the biggest banks and law firms in the City. Bankers at JP Morgan have been the busiest, advising on more takeovers involving UK companies than any other bank this year – a total of 14 deals worth a combined $89.4bn (£67.6bn), according to the LSE. The leading law firm was Slaughter and May, it found. UK bankers have also benefited from soaring bonuses, after the government scrapped a rule capping bonuses at two-times annual salaries in late 2023. Each bank now sets its own upward limit. Big investment banks such as Goldman Sachs now allow performers to be paid up to 25 times their annual salary . The surge in business comes while the banking sector lobbies against paying higher taxes in the UK . Jamie Dimon, the billionaire boss of JP Morgan, has issued several warnings to Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget on 28 October. The industry body UK Finance echoed the view this week. Lenders in the UK currently pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets. The most lucrative deal in the City this year was the £10.6bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by the private equity firm EQT, which is expected to generate more than £370m in fees. Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Deutsche Bank are working on the deal for EQT, while Intertek paid Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Cazenove and PJT Partners. Lawyers at top City firms have started to out-earn some bankers. Partners at the “magic circle” firms Linklaters and Clifford Chance were paid an average of £2.5m and £2.3m respectively in the year to April, their highest ever. A&O Shearman partners were paid £2.2m. At the boutique bank Evercore, which the LSE said had advised on five deals in the UK stock market this year, the firm’s “members” – senior managing directors who are dealmakers – were paid an average of about £2m. Its best-paid member collected £16.2m this year. Overall, dealmaker fees are likely to be even higher this year as the figures do not include deals which did not complete, were rejected or for which documents have not been published – including the £5.7bn takeover of the FTSE 100 airline easyJet by the private equity firm Apollo Global Management, agreed last month . While pay continues to climb in the City, millions of UK households are struggling with the cost of living. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the national secretary at the GMB union, said financial brokers were paid huge sums “while the people who keep this country moving struggle to make ends meet”. “The UK needs to seriously re-examine what we value and hold dear – is it the people who build, who create, who look after us and our loved ones in their hour of need? Or is it a bloated financial sector?” she asked. Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, repeated his call for a windfall tax on lenders’ profits as interest rates have risen , saying that “if banks can afford bonanza payouts for their top brass, they can clearly afford to pay more tax”. “People up and down the country are struggling, and things could get a lot worse with energy prices set to shoot up,” he said. Earlier this month figures from the Office for National Statistics showed that average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, slowed to 3.9% in the three months ended in July, down from 4.1% in the three months ended in June. There are fears that, while dealmakers’ pay is rising on the takeover boom, investment banks could lose out on revenue from their sell-side research and work on flotations as more companies leave London’s stock market and fewer line up to join.

events.title: A tradie tipped this suburb off on a new data centre build. Residents are furious
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Suburban residents protest 15-metre power poles linked to data centre expansion Topic: Urban Development and Planning Industrial power poles 15 metres high have been installed outside Cameron Botterill's house. ( ABC News ) When Cameron Botterill left home one morning, he didn't expect to return to 15-metre power poles soaring above his residential street in Melbourne's inner west. "They're absolute monstrosities," Mr Botterill said. "They're ginormous. They tower above anything else in the suburb and they look very industrial. We're in a residential area here and we definitely did not ask for them to be installed." The power poles went up within a day. ( ABC News ) The new poles are more than twice the height of the 7-metre wooden poles they replaced, and can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, roughly 160 times the voltage that previously ran through his street. In July, Mr Botterill was notified by his electricity distributor, Jemena, that the power would be shut off to allow workers to replace the poles on his street. He didn't find out why until the day the new poles appeared. "I was shocked that this could be installed in a residential area." The site of the NextDC data centre in West Footscray. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The NextDC data centre in nearby West Footscray is already operating, and it's being expanded. One more data centre is proposed for the suburb with another in Spotswood. Jemena says the new power poles are part of its local network upgrade "to help support Melbourne's growing energy needs". "These taller power poles are required mainly for safety reasons," said Michael Brear, a mechanical engineering professor at the University of Melbourne. "When you have a large electrical load like a data centre, you supply it most economically at a higher voltage than typically you would in your home. On streets where the poles have been installed in Melbourne's inner west, there is a strikingly consistent complaint: residents didn't know the change was happening. The power levels required for data centres mean old 7-metre wooden poles have to be replaced. ( ABC News ) In response to questions from 7.30, Jemena said: "We have heard feedback from residents and other stakeholders that our communication and engagement could have been better, and we are taking that feedback seriously." The company told 7.30 it has "paused works and [is] taking the time to listen to the community to understand their concerns". Paul Tyndale was one of those caught by surprise when Jemena crews disconnected his power in the inner west suburb of Spotswood to install a new taller pole. It was only then his family found out a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away. Paul Tyndale found out from a tradie that a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away from his home. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) "We found out about the data centre when the tradie who was disconnecting our house told my partner, 'This is for the new data centre,'" he said. GreenSquare, the company behind the proposed Spotswood Data Centre, now states on its website that the Spotswood poles are not part of its proposal and "are separate electricity network infrastructure works". On Sanderson Street in Yarraville, residents decided to fight back. After neighbours saw 15-metre poles go up a few blocks over, they knew their block was next. Residents on Sanderson Street saw the 15-metre poles going up nearby. ( Supplied ) On the day Jemena crews showed up in August, residents left cars and bins out to block equipment needed to install the poles. Some taped notes on car windows explaining the protest action. Residents on Sanderson Street left cars out to block the equipment needed to install the poles. ( Supplied ) "We were all just really caught off guard and just felt like it was really unfair that we weren't told about what was happening," resident Katrina Dardha said. Eventually, unable to get their equipment in position, the crews filled in the holes they had prepared for upgraded power poles and left. Milco Bogoevski (second from the right) and his neighbours staged a protest to stop the power poles from going up in their street. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant ) "Everyone decided this is not happening on our watch," resident Milco Bogoevski said. "If you stay quiet, it's at your own peril. events.title: Poland is racing ahead with military spending – but will it help or damage its economic growth story?
events.summary: In the first article in a series on the Polish economy, we look at the country’s defence boom and its implications A short distance north from Warsaw along the Vistula river, camouflaged missile launchers roll through the quiet village of Czosnów. As recently as two years ago, their destination – a hi-tech weapons facility opened this month – had been a cornfield. Now, as Poland drives up defence investment at one of the fastest rates in the developed world, this rural spot has been transformed amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement. “Everyone has had to move twice as fast to meet the Polish needs,” says Jim Price, the managing director of MBDA Polska, the local subsidiary of the European multinational arms group. Based in the UK, the former Royal Marine says Poland is shifting from importing its weapons to manufacturing them at home. “When it became clear there is a need to defend Nato’s eastern flank, in the event of a war itself, they needed to be able to do things in the blink of an eye. So we decided to invest in-the country to create a facility. We had to build up our Polish subsidiary – and that means Polish jobs.” Poland’s defence budget has grown at a blistering pace. Since Vladimir Putin ordered Russian troops into Ukraine almost five years ago, spending as a share of Polish gross domestic product (GDP ) has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. In cash terms, this equates to $53bn (£39.8bn), the fourth-highest in the EU after Germany, France and Italy. Attention in Warsaw is clearly focused on the risk of an imminent Russian test of Nato resolve. However, there is also another motive: growing the economy. Inside the soundproofed, airlock-style doors enclosing his office in Warsaw, Marcin Bosacki, Poland’s deputy foreign minister, says Russian aggression is heavily influencing the Polish government’s plans for economic development and cooperation with EU and Nato allies. “[It] is clearly benefiting Polish security; Polish defence, and the Polish economy as well,” he says. Strengthening economic ties in the pursuit of military readiness would discourage Putin (“a traditional Russian imperialist”) from attacking Nato, Bosacki adds. “The only thing which Putin understands is solidarity and power. And so the more we are united and strong, the less likely the outcome of more aggressive Russian provocations against Nato member states is.” Hope remains for a diplomatic solution. This month, Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Next month, further negotiations are scheduled in Abu Dhabi. However, diplomatic sources believe Russia is unlikely to cede ground – rendering Nato’s demonstrations of military readiness critical. History shows defence and economics are closely intertwined. Statisticians first devised GDP as a metric in response to the 1930s Great Depression and needs of wartime planning to gauge the capacity of an economy. Poland has been through an economic miracle since the Solidarność (solidarity) movement that arose from the Gdańsk shipyard strikes paved the way for its transition from communism almost four decades ago. Living standards have shot up from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year. Joining the EU in 2004 and securing catch-up funds from Brussels – which was spent on new roads, railways, and other productivity-enhancing infrastructure – also helped. Annual output surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, with Poland among the fastest-growing EU countries at an annualised rate of 3.9% in the second quarter despite the global headwinds caused by the Iran war . However, Poland’s defence boom is not cost-free. Nor has economic development helped it avoid political polarisation. The rising military budget is among the reasons why Poland is predicted to run the biggest fiscal deficit in the EU next year, at 7.1% of GDP. Last week, Moody’s downgraded the country’s long-term sovereign credit rating to the lowest level since 2002, amid an apparent lack of willingness to rebuild fiscal buffers. Leszek Kąsek, a Warsaw-based economist at ING Bank, said: “This path is not sustainable. You should ask people if Poland can maintain its growth story and whether politicians will be ready to adjust?” Wedged between larger neighbours it has been subjugated twice within living memory, Poles are uneasy about national security. But despite its economic turnaround under EU membership, and as it secures billions of euros in defence funds from Brussels, support for Eurosceptic politics remains. In the run-up to the general election next year, the defence of the country, support for Ukraine and EU relations will be highly politically charged. Outside the foreign ministry in Warsaw, protesters wave placards in a “Poles for peace” nationalist rally, organised by rightwing politicians opposed to the EU and its support for Ukraine.
